These are the animals people most want to see photographed

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions.
  • It has been revealed that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Substantial Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo.
  • According to recent reports, however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Fresh Major Five” for wildlife photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability problems and to inspire positive action.

It has been revealed that originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Substantial Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

According to recent reports, however, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “Fresh Major Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The Latest Substantial 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green notes that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on challenges impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he indicates.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”.

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change.

Recent findings suggest that in total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, indicates Green.

Industry observers note that “I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”.

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “Fresh Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “Latest Major 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” indicates Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds.

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

According to recent reports, “I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she remarked.

“The Upcoming Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking into one bedside gadget. And for the first time, it’s going on sale (early) as a Black Friday deal.

From November 19 through November 20, the Sleep Clock is 25 percent off at Hatch and Amazon. Normally $250, it’s down to $188, which is just $18 more than the Hatch Restore 3’s $170 retail price. And unlike its predecessor, the newer Hatch adds passive sleep monitoring, which is pretty compelling for anyone who hates wearing wearables to bed. Or maybe you’re like me and occasionally forget to wear your Oura Ring to bed, in which case, you wouldn’t have to worry because the Hatch is already quietly tracking your sleep in the background.

I’ve been testing the Hatch Sleep Clock for over two months, and it’s earned a permanent spot on my nightstand. As someone who already wears a smart ring and smartwatch to bed, I’m not exactly short on sleep-tracking data. But I’ve never owned a sunrise alarm clock, and I instantly became a convert. Unlike my iPhone or Amazon Echo Dot, it doesn’t wake me up by blaring an obnoxious alarm in my pitch-black bedroom. Instead, it gradually illuminates the room within my scheduled wake-up time. You can customize the sunrise's duration and brightness, and pair it with a soundscape of your choosing. It truly makes getting out of bed feel less jarring, especially as the mornings get darker.

Recent findings suggest that most notably, the Sleep Clock also doubles as a contactless sleep tracker, using a built-in motion sensor to detect your movements and breathing throughout the night. I compared its readings against my Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12, and while sleep duration estimates were generally aligned, the sleep-stage readings were less consistent. The device doesn’t measure physiological metrics like heart rate, and it can’t detect snoring or other audio-based sleep disruptions. I also found that placement significantly matters. My nightstand tends to collect clutter, so I had to rearrange my trinkets to make room for the clock.

Each morning, the Hatch app gives you a breakdown of when you went to bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and how much time you spent in different sleep stages. The color-coded reports are easy to understand without burying me in random metrics. Plus, unlike most sleep trackers, Hatch doesn't require a subscription to access your sleep data. (You will need that Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) if you want to access the full audio library, however.).

It has been revealed that overall, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the best all-in-one bedside device. I wouldn’t recommend replacing your dedicated wearable with it if detailed health tracking is your priority. But if you’ve been wanting a sunrise alarm clock that can also offer a little insight into your sleep, do not sleep on this Black Friday deal.

If you don’t care for sleep tracking, Hatch is also offering discounts on several other products across its lineup.

  • Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine.

Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.

Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk mentioned he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also noted Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.

In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".

Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," mentioned Mudryk.

"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong.".

Mudryk also mentioned the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.

BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago.
  • According to recent reports, as a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps.
  • To help solve this problem, Thomas A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

According to recent reports, as a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a upcoming tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life.

According to recent reports, to build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Industry observers note that using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced newly introduced scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill notable gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding.

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

It has been revealed that to help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries.

Sources indicate that by highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the newly introduced approach could help paleontologists blueprint more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," states SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

Industry observers note that "But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically.".

Industry observers note that materials provided by Staatliche Naturwissenschaftliche Sammlungen Bayerns. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its upcoming $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed organization's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

According to recent reports, reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

It has been revealed that "It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh remarked during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell.".

Recent findings suggest that keogh stated achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the firm can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase.".

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also stated the organization is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh noted the organization is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

It has been revealed that "The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through.".

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

Latest Update: Wael Mohya could make German football history at 17

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer.
  • Industry observers note that "Of course, I was absolutely thrilled.
  • "And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon.

Industry observers note that "Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya mentioned.

"And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud.".

According to recent reports, mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager noted in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

The youngster, who was born in a small town east of Düsseldorf, smiles and laughs a lot in interviews. He is always friendly, and in a good mood. On the field, too, he exudes the lightheartedness and carefree spirit of a 17-year-old.

Sources indicate that as a technically skilled and creative player, Mohya often seeks out one-on-one situations and puts his opponents under pressure with quick dribbles. In nine Bundesliga appearances this season, Mohya has scored twice and delivered one assist.

Industry observers note that "He's so cool and just plays really well. It's fun to watch him," Borussia coach Alexander Blessin noted recently.

In a recent development, "Wael brings a lot to the team with his laid-back attitude on the field. He's not afraid to take risks, no matter how much pressure there is," added Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder at a talk show on Sport1.

Borussia Mönchengladbach has been Mohya's sporting home since he was seven years old. Last season, previous head coach Eugen Polanski promoted him to the first team, and in December 2025, Mohya made his Bundesliga debut. Against Wolfsburg, aged 16 years and 347 days old, he became the youngest Bundesliga player in the club's history.

Industry observers note that mohya also recently completed a voluntary social year at an elementary school in Mönchengladbach. This is a program in Germany for young people who volunteer in the social sector — at hospitals, schools, or nursing homes, for example — for about six to 18 months. They gain work experience, help others, and earn a little money.

Recent findings suggest that at the school's open all-day care program, Mohya helped serve meals, assisted children with their homework, and played with them. That's also where his nickname comes from. Because a girl hadn't understood his first name correctly or couldn't pronounce it, she called him "Waffel." Now, that name has stuck.

It has been revealed that even before being called up to the Germany team, clubs in the Bundesliga and across Europe's top leagues had taken notice of Mohya and were trying to sign him. His contract with Borussia Mönchengladbach runs through 2028.

With Gladbach currently in a relegation battle, his future appears likely to be elsewhere. If the club wants to generate transfer revenue from its biggest talent, next summer would likely be the opportunity to sell him — unless he extends his contract with Borussia.

Recent findings suggest that the 17-year-old's career is managed by his parents. Whichever club can convince them that their son is in good hands and help him reach his full potential likely has the best chance of securing Mohya's signing.

Mohya himself says he doesn't even know how much he's presently earning at Gladbach.

Sources indicate that "My parents take care of all that," he told Bild recently. "I get a monthly allowance, which is more than enough for me.".

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp recently revealed how much he had enjoyed his conversations with the youngster.

"The conversations I had with him were great," Klopp noted with a laugh. "I wasn't that confident at 17, but then again, I wasn't that good either.".

Since Mohya's parents are from Morocco, their son also holds Moroccan citizenship. As a result, he could have played for Morocco, but he has now decided against it. In fact, the Moroccan football association had been actively courting Mohya as early as last year and had already reached out to him in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.

Now, like Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib, Mohya will continue to play in the German jersey, unlike Schalke's Soufiane El-Faouzi, who chose Morocco, or Bayer Leverkusen's Ibrahim Maza, who likely would have been selected by Klopp as well if he hadn't already opted for Algeria.

Sources indicate that for Mohya, who played for Germany's youth teams from the U16s through to the U21s, the door to Morocco remains open, even if he does play for Germany. According to FIFA regulations, players under the age of 21 can change national teams before their fourth international match (whether a competitive or friendly match), provided that none of those matches take place during a World Cup or a continental tournament such as the European Championship, Copa America, or Africa Cup of Nations.

Industry observers note that if Mohya plays in the upcoming UEFA Nations League games in Serbia or against the Netherlands, another record is on the horizon. Although there were two even younger players who made their debuts in the Germany jersey — Willy Baumgärtner in 1908 (at 17 years and 104 days) and Marius Hiller in 1910 (at 17 years and 241 days) — the era in which they debuted is hardly comparable. And so, while Wael Mohya would rank third overall on the list, he would become the youngest Germany player in the modern era. The youngest to date was Hamburg legend Uwe Seeler in 1954, aged 17 years and 345 days.

Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.
  • Sources indicate that the annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov.
  • Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

Sources indicate that the annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

Recent findings suggest that the meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows.".

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

Sources indicate that turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this. -- November 18, 2026 York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3November 18, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that this phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, Latest Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

According to recent reports, "But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog.".

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

In a recent development, "One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

さきほど、しし座流星群の大火球が流れました。2026年11月19日4時35分2秒に、平塚から北の低い空に向けたカメラでとらえた様子です。緑色のアフターグローからオレンジ色の永続痕まで、美しく色を変化させました。 https://t.co/Q5ihqCPtX2November 18, 2026.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

It has been revealed that elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

昨夜から今朝にかけて捉えた流星は正味92個でした。 11/18 22:17 〜 11/19 05:40 埼玉県中央から #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 https://t.co/jRzsHdQ7MVNovember 19, 2026.

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

昨夜の流星とスプライト、初めて同じタイミングで撮れた。 11/19 02:19:36 埼玉県中央から北西の空 #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 #スプライト https://t.co/LBipTuoM0LNovember 19, 2026.

The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak.

On Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky.

Meteors from last night/this morning. Cropped to show detail. A lot of possible Leonids. The Leonid meteor shower is active and peaks the night of 11/17-11/18. https://t.co/s7YsvKdvECNovember 15, 2026.

According to recent reports, A likely Leonid meteor from yesterday morning. The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Good luck if you go out to watch. https://t.co/xxbEV32NQlNovember 17, 2026.

If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

#59227. Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1046 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection.
  • According to recent reports, scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses.
  • Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. Latest research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

According to recent reports, scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to latest threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage.

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

Sources indicate that using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

Industry observers note that according to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved.".

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an key role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

In a recent development, these structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to fresh challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," notes Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state.".

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage.

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with upcoming challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications.

Sources indicate that the findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise notable questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

Recent findings suggest that the research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

Recent findings suggest that "The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society.".

  • The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology tech giant announced a newly introduced studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration.

The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May.

"We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties.".

This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The organization is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December.

It has been revealed that each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment.

Industry observers note that in this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor.

Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film.

Industry observers note that "We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner.".

Recent findings suggest that the premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans.

Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies.

"What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice mentioned. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business.".

It has been revealed that and Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise releases, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands.

Correction: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Alexis Scalice's name.

Latest Update: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fresh forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife.
  • Recent findings suggest that the evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago.
  • Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fresh forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling newly introduced support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?".

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings.

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," said Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans.".

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.".

According to recent reports, despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths.

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

Sources indicate that the results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls showed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing key newly introduced evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Industry observers note that accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

Additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal Fresh Clues to Egypt's Dark Past.

The findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve important clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" remarked Campbell. "Still, this study demonstrates how much latest information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Empire State Building glowed in glittering gold last night (Nov. 17) to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hitting one light-day from Earth. And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display.

Industry observers note that today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space.

Recent findings suggest that to celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in Upcoming York City lit up in gold. This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

It has been revealed that and the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. The Space Needle in Seattle, Washington, and both the Willis Tower and the Skydeck Chicago in Chicago, Illinois have all been illuminated gold to mark the milestone.

It has been revealed that the Golden Record that these gold glowing buildings are referencing serves as an inanimate ambassador for Earth, carrying information about humanity, our planet, the other species who live here, the languages we speak, the music we listen to and so much more. It even includes instructions for building a record player to play the record.

The Voyager mission has, and continues to, make incredible scientific discoveries and observations throughout our solar system and now in interstellar space. But this Golden Record provides an additional aspect to the mission that connects us here on Earth to whatever unknown life may exist out there.

If some sort of life forms out in the cosmos were to ever come across Voyager and its Golden Record at any point in the distant future, they might learn a little bit about our small blue dot.

Jennifer Lopez might one day get off the floor, but she wants her kids to remember all of her steps.

The “On the Floor” singer recently shared that she produced her upcoming concert special The JLO Show partially to serve as a piece of legacy for her and ex Marc Anthony’s 18-year-old kids Max and Emme.

“I would want it to be something that my kids could watch and go, ‘Oh, that’s who mom was,’” Lopez told E! News’ Lauren Herbert in an exclusive interview Nov. 19, noting that she hopes it continues through future generations. “‘That’s who grandma was, that’s who great grandma was.’ They can have this forever and they can see my heart, my soul, my story.”.

And while the concert film—which premieres on CBS and Paramount+ on Nov. 26 at 8 p.m. ET—is a joyous highlight of her career, she wanted to make sure it was an authentic piece of her legacy, too.

“Who I was as an entertainer but also who I was as a human and my journey,” she added, so that her kids, “always know that they can go through life and go through hard things and wonderful things and still come out the other side stronger and happier.”.

Of course, The JLO Show—a filmed taping of one of her shows during her recently-concluded residency at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas—is mostly about having fun.

“For me, as an entertainer, my job is to make sure everybody enjoys themselves and has a good time,” she added. “Everything about the show is put together to tell a story.”.

After putting the project together, the 57-year-old emphasized it was hard to even identify how much she got out of the experience.

“It’s everything you hope for,” she mused. “Like, people see what you’re trying to say in the most beautiful ways which is to be inspired and to empower them.”.

While the Maid in Manhattan actress is uncertain of her next step, she shared that she also hopes The JLO Show acts as a time capsule for her time as a pop star.

Recent findings suggest that “When I toured that summer before we did this show, I was thinking like, ‘what if this is the last show I ever do? What if I don’t do anything? What if I never tour again?’ she explained, “What if this or what if that. If it was, what do I want this show to be?’”.

And so, it turned into an amalgamation of everything Lopez stands for, as well as a future gift for her kids. For a deeper look into her bond with her kids over the years, keep reading….

Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine.
  • The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful latest way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline.
  • In a recent development, to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers.".

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful latest way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

In a recent development, to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

The results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss.

In a recent development, the new scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

According to recent reports, "We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," stated Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.".

Zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

According to recent reports, transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang noted. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be.".

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

Zhang recognized that this approach could overlook important biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he said. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.".

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

The Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

Recent findings suggest that they examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

According to recent reports, the comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas indicated greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Recent findings suggest that using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance.

The team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

It has been revealed that at the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores showed no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, key differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that the available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

People whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

In a recent development, "We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao noted. "Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.".

A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging.

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements showed some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he noted.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially shows a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

Industry observers note that for example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

Industry observers note that importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

According to recent reports, his research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he stated. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.".

Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially notable newly introduced direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, legacy retailer Gap Inc.
  • Sources indicate that it was a newly created role as the firm tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform.
  • Sources indicate that "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.

Sources indicate that it was a newly created role as the firm tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye.

Sources indicate that "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it.".

She said it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.

"Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson said at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation.".

Sources indicate that in another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the manufacturer, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap.

In a recent development, "I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," noted Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form.".

Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman said, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing.

"Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he noted.

Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.

But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts noted audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original.

The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.

As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.

According to recent reports, "The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience.".

Sources indicate that at the same time, he noted, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.

The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.

Recent findings suggest that "The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael noted. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly.".

Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, remarked Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

Recent findings suggest that "I think it's a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you're seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies," he noted. "I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content.".

That's where retailers might tap creators, Akaks mentioned, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.

"I do think there's a world where we're going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they're owning together," he stated.

Once those companies get consumers into the store, they're also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick's Sporting Goods offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.

According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach and Ralph Lauren saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers' average basket size.

"The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it's experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow," noted Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.

In a recent development, yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract new ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn't necessarily a given.

"The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics," AlixPartners' Eshelman said. "The fundamentals are still there, and if you're going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can't mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour.".
